meta.title: Who really said "There is nothing to writing. All you do is sit down at a typewriter and bleed"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Hemingway. He never wrote it — first pinned on him in 1973, 12 years after his death. The metaphor traces to sportswriter Red Smith (1949) and Paul Gallico (1946).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is nothing to writing. All you do is sit down at a typewriter and bleed'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Hemingway. First credited to him in 1973, 12 years after his death. The typewriter-and-bleed metaphor traces to Red Smith (1949) and Paul Gallico (1946).

answer.label: Not Ernest Hemingway — a sportswriter’s line, later paraphrased
answer.sourceLine: Ernest Hemingway never wrote this line: it appears in none of his novels, stories, letters, or interviews, and the first person to pin it on him did so in 1973 — twelve years after his death — in William C. Knott’s writing manual The Craft of Fiction, with no source given (Quote Investigator ↗). The metaphor was already old by then: syndicated columnist Walter Winchell reported in 1949 that sportswriter Walter ‘Red’ Smith, asked whether writing a daily column was a chore, dead-panned that “you simply sit down at the typewriter, open your veins, and bleed,” and Paul Gallico had used an earnest version in 1946. The tidy modern wording credited to Hemingway is a later paraphrase with no single documented author.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: 1973 — William C. Knott, The Craft of Fiction

source.excerpt: “Why, no,” dead-panned Red. “You simply sit down at the typewriter, open your veins, and bleed.”
trail: Quote Investigator (Garson O’Toole) traces the saying back to Paul Gallico’s 1946 “open your veins and bleed onto the page” and Red Smith’s 1949 “sit down at the typewriter, open your veins, and bleed,” and finds the first Hemingway credit only in 1973 — concluding there is “no substantive evidence” connecting it to him (quoteinvestigator.com ↗).
The Hemingway Society publicly acknowledges it once featured this quote in error, agreeing with the research that the attribution to Hemingway is unsupported (hemingwaysociety.org ↗).
The line does not appear in Wikiquote’s sourced Hemingway entry — consistent with there being no primary source for it in his work (en.wikiquote.org ↗).
source.excerptNote: Columnist Walter Winchell’s April 1949 report of sportswriter Red Smith — the earliest well-evidenced version of the typewriter-and-bleed line, and the closest documented ancestor of the wording later pinned on Hemingway.

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording — “There is nothing to writing. All you do is sit down at a typewriter and bleed” — has no identified author or first-publication of record; it is a later paraphrase of a metaphor documented for Red Smith (1949) and Paul Gallico (1946). Because its origin as worded is unknown, no copyright status can be responsibly asserted.

author.name: Walter ‘Red’ Smith
author.heading: So who actually said it?
author.bio: Walter Wellesley “Red” Smith was one of the most admired American sports columnists of the 20th century, syndicated nationally and awarded the 1976 Pulitzer Prize for Commentary. Asked in 1949 whether grinding out a daily column was hard, he gave the wry answer — “you simply sit down at the typewriter, open your veins, and bleed” — that is the best-evidenced ancestor of the line later, and wrongly, handed to Hemingway. An even earlier earnest version of the metaphor came from novelist and sportswriter Paul Gallico in 1946.

cite.sourceCitation: Garson O’Toole (Quote Investigator), “Writing Is Easy; You Just Open a Vein and Bleed,” September 14, 2011, quoteinvestigator.com. Earliest documented forms: Paul Gallico (1946); Walter ‘Red’ Smith, quoted by Walter Winchell (1949). Earliest Hemingway attribution: William C. Knott, The Craft of Fiction (1973).

misattribution.heading: A quote with many false fathers
misattribution.intro: This one line has been attached to at least five different writers — almost always long after they could object. The research is unusually clean here, thanks to Quote Investigator and The Hemingway Society.

items.why: First credited to Hemingway only in 1973, twelve years after his death, in William C. Knott’s The Craft of Fiction, with no source. It appears in none of his books, letters, or interviews (Quote Investigator ↗).
Credited with a version in Gene Olson’s 1972 Sweet Agony — again decades after Wolfe’s death and with no supporting evidence (Quote Investigator ↗).
First credited in 1980’s The Writer’s Quotation Book; a widely repeated version, but it postdates the saying’s appearance in print by decades (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The metaphor of “bleeding” at the typewriter is best traced to sportswriter Red Smith (quoted 1949) and, earlier and more earnestly, Paul Gallico (1946) — not Hemingway (The Hemingway Society ↗).

context.heading: Why it sticks to Hemingway
lead: The line has everything a viral writing-quote needs: it is short, tough, a little bloody, and it flatters the idea of the writer as sufferer. Hemingway — terse, macho, endlessly quotable — is the perfect magnet for it, which is exactly why it drifted onto him in the 1970s and never left.

The irony is that the real coiners were newspapermen making a joke about deadline drudgery, not novelists romanticizing art. Red Smith’s 1949 dead-pan and Paul Gallico’s 1946 line were about the daily grind of filing copy — humble origins the polished “Hemingway” version conveniently erases.
context.pull: He never wrote it. The first person to blame Hemingway did so in 1973 — twelve years after Hemingway died.
